text: Fifteen minutes. That's how long it took this quiet river in Zion to carry nearly fifty times more water. September fourteenth, twenty fifteen: seven canyoneers were inside Keyhole Canyon. None came out. The full story is in Zion's Deadliest Day, on our YouTube channel.

Seventy-one feet per mile. That's how fast the Virgin River drops through Zion. The Mississippi drops about an inch. And these walls are bare sandstone, so a sudden storm doesn't soak in. It runs off, and every side canyon becomes a funnel. This small river carries about a million tons of rock and sand out of the park every year, most of it during floods. The floods aren't an accident here. They're how the canyon was made. Full documentary: Zion's Deadliest Day, on YouTube.

In the Narrows, the trail is the river. We hiked it top to bottom in November twenty twenty-one. Walls a thousand feet high, and in places only twenty to thirty feet apart. When the water rises in here, there's often nowhere to climb. Watch Zion's Deadliest Day on our channel.

Four nights on a ledge above a roaring waterfall. July nineteen ninety-three: a church group, three leaders and five teenage boys, set out to descend Kolob Creek in Zion. The water was far higher than they expected. Two of the leaders drowned. The last adult and the five boys climbed onto a ledge above the torrent, and waited. Four nights. Rescuers finally winched them out, almost fifteen hundred feet. All six survived. The full story is in Zion's Deadliest Day, on YouTube.

A dog died an hour after playing in this river. Fourth of July, twenty twenty. Park scientists found a microbe in the algae making a nerve toxin, far above safe levels. Never let your dog drink from the Virgin River. Full documentary: Zion's Deadliest Day.

At least seventeen deaths on one trail. Angels Landing, Zion. The last half mile follows a spine of rock with sheer drops on both sides, and for much of it the only thing to hold is a chain bolted into the stone. We climbed it in twenty twenty-one, and the top stands nearly fifteen hundred feet above the river. Here's the strange part: many of the falls didn't happen on the chains at all. They happened where people felt safe. Watch Zion's Deadliest Day on our channel.

Eight percent. On the busiest days, those were your odds of winning a permit to climb Angels Landing. Since twenty twenty-two the park gives them out by lottery, nearly four hundred thousand in two years. Full story: Zion's Deadliest Day, on YouTube.

Almost five tons of human waste. That's what park crews hauled off the toilets at Scout Lookout, just below the Angels Landing chains, in twenty twenty-one. That's what five million visitors look like. Watch Zion's Deadliest Day on our channel.

Four thousand visitors became five million. In nineteen twenty, fewer than four thousand people visited Zion. In twenty twenty-one, more than five million did, a record. Most leave with nothing but photographs. But rangers here answer hundreds of emergency calls every year, because the things that make Zion beautiful, the water and the rock, never stop moving. Sometimes they move all at once. The full story is in Zion's Deadliest Day, on YouTube.

This hotel sits on the bottom of a lake. The flat valley floor where Zion Lodge stands was left behind when a whole mountainside collapsed into the canyon. That's our next documentary: The Day the Mountain Fell.
